Triggers.value: Specific body parts associated with the event
Night-time or waking up in the dark

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Going to sleep or lying in the dark

Memory.value: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

issues.item: Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
issues.explanation: 'Always plan an escape route before entering a place' implies a persistent current external-danger / entrapment threat style that is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on intrusive sensory memory linked to the child's illness (body parts, darkness, songs; reliving, fragments, present-tense memory). For trauma of a child's life-threatening illness, this strategy is clinically much less coherent than avoidance/sleep delay, and it is not supported by any Threat or Appraisal items. Given the formulation, Triggers and Memory are strongly linked, but this item reflects a different syndrome focus (situational escape/safety behavior) not represented elsewhere in the selected nodes.

vignette:
Bounyong Phommasack is a 42-year-old Lao American farmer who lives with his wife on a small vegetable operation in the Central Valley of California. He was referred for psychological assessment after his wife contacted a community health worker, concerned that her husband had not slept properly in nearly eight months and had become increasingly withdrawn from her, from their children, and from the neighbors and extended family who form the social fabric of their rural community.

The precipitating event occurred the previous winter, when Bounyong and his wife discovered their seven-year-old son, Keo, unresponsive in his bed one morning. The boy had developed a severe bacterial infection that had gone undetected for several days, and by the time the ambulance arrived he was seizing. Bounyong rode with him to the hospital and spent the next eleven days in the pediatric intensive care unit, watching his son connected to monitors and IV lines, his small body swollen and mottled with the effort of fighting the infection. There was a night-the fourth or fifth, Bounyong could no longer be certain-when a nurse called him urgently to the bedside and he saw Keo's arm limp against the bedrail, the skin discolored at the crook of the elbow where the IV had infiltrated. A physician spoke words about organ function and probabilities. Keo eventually recovered fully, but something in Bounyong did not close behind him when they finally drove home.

In the weeks that followed, the memory refused to behave like something that had ended. Bounyong described it in his first session as feeling less like remembering and more like being pulled back without warning - a fragment of the PICU appearing suddenly and completely, the beeping of monitors, the particular pallor of Keo's forearm, and then gone, leaving him standing in a field row or at the kitchen table with his heart hammering. He was insistent on one point: it did not feel like the past. It felt like now, like something still unfolding, and no amount of reminding himself that Keo was currently outside kicking a soccer ball seemed to reach whatever part of him held the memory.

Certain things reliably pulled these fragments forward. The sight of a child's arm - or his own - in a particular position, the inner elbow visible, was enough. He had begun wearing long sleeves on the farm regardless of the heat, and he found himself looking away when his children reached across the dinner table. A Lao pop song that had been playing softly from a phone in the waiting room during one of the worst nights had become unbearable to him; he left a family gathering in March when a relative played something that shared its tempo and key.

Night had become its own problem. The darkness of the bedroom carried a weight that Bounyong struggled to articulate, but he associated the worst of those hospital nights with waking in the dim ward, disoriented, and believing for several seconds each time that Keo had already died. He had come to believe that falling asleep before exhaustion fully overtook him was not something he could safely do, and so he stayed up well past midnight most nights, working on equipment in the barn or watching television at low volume, waiting until he was certain sleep would take him immediately and completely, before the dark could settle in around him. Even then he sometimes woke at three or four in the morning and lay rigid, certain for a moment that something terrible was still happening somewhere he could not reach.

The consequences had accumulated quietly. His wife handled the children's bedtime routines alone now. Several neighboring farmers had stopped dropping by, put off by Bounyong's curtness on the occasions when they did visit; he found conversation effortful and company intrusive in a way he could not explain to himself or to them. His harvest this past season was smaller than it should have been, because there were mornings he could not organize his thinking well enough to direct his workers efficiently.

What finally brought him in was a conversation with Keo, who asked his father one evening why he never laughed anymore. Bounyong could not answer the boy. What he most feared, sitting across from the clinician at intake, was that something had permanently changed in him - and what he most hoped, though he said it quietly and without much conviction, was that it had not.
